A.name: Choosing a partner and getting started
A.text: How people choose a business partner, why they go into partnership at all, and what happens in the first months while a group of co-owners is still taking shape. Two special cases belong here as well: a hired manager who is offered a stake, and an investor's view of a founding team. The section's common thread: if a partnership can be avoided, avoid it; if it cannot, start with agreements rather than a logo.

B.name: Partnership agreement and money
B.text: What a partnership agreement is, how it differs from a document and from a contract, why partners put off writing it down for years and what that costs them. The practical money questions live here too: how to split equity when contributions differ, how to agree on salaries, dividends and spending limits, and which scenarios of failure, windfall and a partner's departure to settle in advance. The section rests on one idea: the law serves only one function of an agreement; the rest the partners work out themselves.

C.name: Relationships and trust
C.text: How relationships between co-owners work in the space between formal decisions: trust, expectations and the inevitable disappointment, diverging pictures of reality, the roles each partner takes on, and the price of the "hero" who overworks. The materials show that trust does not replace structure, and that expectations and disappointment can be managed if they are talked about in time.

D.name: Conflict, misconduct and exit
D.text: What happens when a partnership cracks: where conflicts come from and how to settle disputes short of court; how to recognise misconduct and what internal control protects against it; how a partner leaves the business and why the exit has to be agreed before the start. The section draws on cases from partnership sessions and on data about how often founding teams change.

E.name: Method and tools
E.text: How the author works with co-owners: the partnership session as a structured conversation about how partners will work together, conscious partnership as a skill rather than luck, tools and services for partners, and ideas borrowed from adjacent fields, from psychology and law to sport and film, that help see partnership more clearly.

F.name: Partnership as a phenomenon
F.text: Partnership as the blind spot of business: there is almost no statistics on it, it is rarely studied and usually remembered too late. The section collects data and research on co-owners, founders and unicorns, together with the author's own experience: personal partnerships, mistakes and the conclusions the method is built on.

G.name: Other
G.text: Material outside the partnership theme: notes on the economy and statistics, on LinkedIn and personal brand, announcements of talks and live sessions, personal observations. They show what else the author follows beyond the main subject, and sometimes feed ideas back into it.

choosing-a-business-partner.name: Choosing a business partner
choosing-a-business-partner.text: How to choose a business partner and what to look at before the deal: motives, resources, decision style, willingness to answer direct questions. The author offers question lists, a profiler check and an honest conversation about whether a partnership is needed at all. The key criterion is not the candidate's charm but their ability to reach agreements.

why-people-go-into-partnership.name: Why people go into partnership
why-people-go-into-partnership.text: Why people really go into partnership: for money, resources, the courage to start, the feeling of someone beside them. Hidden motives are rarely spoken aloud and later become a source of disappointment. The materials help name one's own motive and check whether it matches the partner's.

forming-a-partner-team.name: Forming a partner team
forming-a-partner-team.text: What happens while a group of co-owners is still forming: the root problems of the first months, partnerships of more than two people, emergent partnerships that arose on their own. Team stories are examined, from the Wiz founders turning down 23 billion dollars to the bankruptcy of Lilium, along with the agreements needed at the start.

turning-a-manager-into-a-partner.name: Turning a manager into a partner
turning-a-manager-into-a-partner.text: When and how a hired manager becomes a partner: whether a stake can be a reward, what the owner should fix in the agreement, who appoints the CEO when there are several partners. A separate thread covers owners stepping out of operations and why Ukrainian owners are reluctant to share equity with management.

co-founders-through-an-investors-eyes.name: Co-founders through an investor's eyes
co-founders-through-an-investors-eyes.text: How an investor looks at a founding team: what a founders' agreement means to them, why a one-person business does not qualify, what the road to a unicorn costs and how long it takes. Findings from Stanford and venture funds are translated into decisions for partners.

partnership-agreement.name: Partnership agreement
partnership-agreement.text: What a partnership agreement really is: the agreement the partners reach, the document that records it, and the legal contract as its enforceable part. The materials cover the three layers and four functions of an agreement, the limit of legal formalisation, the lawyer's role and how a partnership document differs from a charter. The largest topic in the catalogue.

why-partners-avoid-signing-an-agreement.name: Why partners avoid signing an agreement
why-partners-avoid-signing-an-agreement.text: Why partners put off writing their agreements down for years: faith in friendship and chemistry, fear of the conversation, hope in lawyers and courts. The cost of refusing is examined, from conflict to losing the business, along with why a court protects only a small part of an agreement while the rest rests on the partners themselves.

equity-split-between-partners.name: Equity split between partners
equity-split-between-partners.text: How to split equity when "equal shares" does not work: the three kinds of capital partners contribute, valuing an idea and social capital, the Slicing Pie model, revisiting shares when a partner suddenly asks for more. The materials show that a share is not arithmetic but a recorded agreement about contribution.

money-between-partners.name: Money between partners
money-between-partners.text: Financial agreements between co-owners: the limit up to which a partner decides alone, salary for an operating role kept apart from dividends, access to money, a budget before areas of responsibility, a shared pension fund. The main point: money between partners is a matter of agreement, not trust.

scenario-planning.name: Scenario planning: failure, windfall, a partner dropping out
scenario-planning.text: Which scenarios partners should rehearse in advance: failure, windfall, a partner dropping out through illness, death or the wish to leave, crisis and turbulence. Scenario planning gives an agreed course of action for the moment when negotiating under stress is too late. Examples come from sessions and stories such as a Ferrari bought by five people.

trust-between-partners.name: Trust between partners
trust-between-partners.text: What trust between partners is and why it does not replace structure: trust takes long to build, is lost in an instant and speeds up work while it lasts. The materials show how trust relates to agreements, leadership and the willingness to write rules down, and why "we trust each other" is no argument against an agreement.

partner-expectations.name: Partner expectations
partner-expectations.text: Where partners' expectations come from and why they are so hard to say aloud: starting optimism, the image of an ideal partner, unspoken hopes. Managing expectations means revisiting agreements regularly and talking honestly about what each partner really wants.

disappointment-in-a-partnership.name: Disappointment in a partnership
disappointment-in-a-partnership.text: How disappointment arises in a partnership: the formula of expectations versus reality, suddenness, an accumulation of small things, unequal contribution with equal shares. A series on managing disappointment, lowering its potential and keeping it from destroying the relationship and the business.

when-partners-see-different-realities.name: When partners see different realities
when-partners-see-different-realities.text: Why partners see the same events differently: the Thomas theorem, the different experience of a corporate executive and an entrepreneur, "napkin" agreements each understood in their own way. The materials offer a procedure for synchronising worldviews and methods for resolving divergence.

the-hero-partner-and-overwork.name: The hero partner and overwork
the-hero-partner-and-overwork.text: The "hero" partner who carries everything alone: why that is dangerous for the business and for the person, why dependence on one individual scares investors off, how to agree on work-life balance. With data on overwork in Europe and court practice.

the-three-roles-of-a-co-owner.name: The three roles of a co-owner
the-three-roles-of-a-co-owner.text: A co-owner can be owner, manager and executor at once, with different rights, rewards and competences in each role. The three-roles frame clarifies what dividends pay for and what salary and bonus pay for, how partners report to each other, and what to do when a partner falls short in one of the roles.

managing-partner-relationships.name: Managing partner relationships
managing-partner-relationships.text: How to keep a partnership in working order: regularly revisiting agreements, leadership inside the partnership, the illusions that destroy it, signs of crisis, silence as the main risk. Materials on the idea that a partnership has to be managed just like the business.

conflicts-between-partners.name: Conflicts between partners
conflicts-between-partners.text: Where conflicts between partners come from and how to resolve them short of court: the limit of acceptable risk, differing views, disregard for each other's time, silence instead of conversation. Real stories of co-owner conflicts are examined together with ways to resolve them, including mediation and the partnership session.

partner-misconduct-and-internal-control.name: Partner misconduct and internal control
partner-misconduct-and-internal-control.text: Partner misconduct and protection against it: what deception is made of, what evil looks like in a partnership, what to do with a "sleeping" partner, who is to blame when a partner exploits your hard situation. Clear agreements and internal control are needed not out of distrust but as rules of the game.

a-partners-exit-from-the-business.name: A partner's exit from the business
a-partners-exit-from-the-business.text: How a partner leaves the business and why the exit must be agreed before the start: valuing the shares, a "prenup" for partners, written exit scenarios, non-compete and no-poach clauses. With data on how often founding teams change in the first years.

partnership-session.name: Partnership session
partnership-session.text: The partnership session is a structured conversation between co-owners and a facilitator about how they will work together: goals, roles, money, scenarios, rules for revision. Materials on what happens in a session, where its value lies, which clients the author turns down, and why conflicts more often stem from processes than from people.

conscious-partnership.name: Conscious partnership
conscious-partnership.text: Conscious partnership is the approach that treats partnership as a skill and a structure rather than luck, friendship or chemistry. Nobody is born a partner, agreeing is learned, and the ceiling of a partnership is set by the partners' skills, not the contract. Materials on how to think about a partnership before it starts to hurt.

tools-and-services.name: Tools and services
tools-and-services.text: Tools and services for co-owners: question lists for a partner, tension diagnostics, the Partner Journey Map, a profiler check, the partnership session and consultations. Also notes on how the author works with clients, which clients get turned down, and how AI is changing attitudes to expert work.

ideas-from-adjacent-fields.name: Ideas from adjacent fields
ideas-from-adjacent-fields.text: Ideas from psychology, law, economics, sport, film and history applied to business partnership: the Peter principle, compartmentalisation, negotiation techniques, court cases, films about partners. The broadest topic in the catalogue, where the author tests which borrowed experience works for co-owners.

partnership-the-blind-spot-of-business.name: Partnership: the blind spot of business
partnership-the-blind-spot-of-business.text: Partnership as the blind spot of business: there is almost no statistics on co-owners, certainly not in Ukraine, only those already burned think seriously about an agreement, and court protection turns out weaker than it seems. A series of materials and polls through which the author gathers first-hand data on partnerships.

data-and-research.name: Data and research
data-and-research.text: Data and research on partners, founders and unicorns: findings from Stanford, Carta, venture funds and surveys. How many founders leave in the first years, what co-owners really fight about, who creates unicorns and how often. Every figure comes with its source.

the-authors-own-partnerships.name: The author's own partnerships
the-authors-own-partnerships.text: The author's own experience: personal partnerships, mistakes, crises and the conclusions the partnership-session method is built on. Stories about agreeing on limits, exit and revision of terms, and why the consultant first tries to talk people out of a partnership.

economy-and-statistics.name: Economy and statistics
economy-and-statistics.text: Notes on the economy and statistics outside the partnership theme: wage arrears, IT services exports, the distribution of wealth, salaries by city, lobbying. The author reads these figures the same way as partnership data: with a source and the question of what follows.

linkedin-and-personal-brand.name: LinkedIn and personal brand
linkedin-and-personal-brand.text: On LinkedIn and personal brand: how the algorithms see an expert, publicity versus privacy, fame and money, cold messages, author rankings. The author's observations about the platform where most of the material first appears.

talks-and-interviews.name: Talks and interviews
talks-and-interviews.text: Talks, live sessions, podcasts and in-person meetings about partnership: announcements, entrepreneurs' questions from the floor, audience response. Materials on how the partnership theme sounds live and what people ask about it.

personal-notes.name: Personal notes
personal-notes.text: The author's personal notes: observations on professionalism, decisions, inspiration, books and films, sometimes with no direct link to partnership. Short texts that show how the author thinks.

blog-pravo-samo-sebe-ne-vikonuye-tri-kro.title: What really stands behind the words 'if anything goes wrong, we'll go to court'?
blog-pravo-samo-sebe-ne-vikonuye-tri-kro.text: The phrase hides three separate steps: a court ruling, its enforcement and the bank debiting the money, and at each one the outcome depends on a judge, an enforcement officer and a bank the partners never chose. Most disputes never get there, so the law works as a shadow.

li-7521136758562918400.title: Why should partners sign agreements a court will not enforce?
li-7521136758562918400.text: A signature does three things before any court gets involved: acknowledgement (discussed is not agreed), a promise to the person sitting next to you, and a reference point in a dispute. The legal function only switches on in conflict, so changed agreements should be re-signed.

blog-odin-advokat-ne-mozhet-zashhishhat-.title: Why can't one lawyer draw up an agreement "for both" partners?
blog-odin-advokat-ne-mozhet-zashhishhat-.text: The rules of the legal profession bar a lawyer from acting for parties with conflicting interests, and on shares, buyout and non-compete partners' interests diverge by default. In a dispute, the drafting lawyer cannot defend one partner without the other's consent.

li-7520394786332270592.title: Up to what amount may a partner decide alone?
li-7520394786332270592.text: Up to a sum named in advance; above it decisions are made together, and the author holds that whoever exceeds the limit covers the loss. The case: a 2018 credit shipment worth $70,000, a buyer who vanished, and a loss split by shares.

protocol-ua-domovlenist-dokument-i-dogov.title: Where does the partners' agreement end and the lawyer's work begin?
protocol-ua-domovlenist-dokument-i-dogov.text: Partners come to a lawyer "for a contract" before agreeing among themselves and get a template. The article separates agreement, document and contract: the lawyer drafts only the enforceable layer; the other two the partners work out themselves.
protocol-ua-domovlenist-dokument-i-dogov.o: Домовленість, документ і договір у діловому партнерстві

blog-podpis-pod-partnerskim-soglasheniem.title: What does a signature under a partnership agreement do besides legal force?
blog-podpis-pod-partnerskim-soglasheniem.text: A signature does four things: it confirms that what was discussed became an agreement, turns it into a promise, sets a reference point for future disputes and only in conflict gives legal force. The first three work from day one of the partnership.

li-7517843125097267202.title: Where does each partner's limit of acceptable risk lie?
li-7517843125097267202.text: It differs for everyone, from mortgaging a house to dealing with criminals to save the business, and it is most dangerous to discuss it first in a crisis. The author insists a partnership session settle in advance what partners will never do.

li-7516792129034235904.title: Why does "we have everything on paper" not mean partners have an agreement?
li-7516792129034235904.text: An agreement does four jobs: declares values, aligns scenarios, anchors negotiations and makes terms enforceable in court, and the law serves only the last. Charter and shareholder agreement cover that one; the first three the partners must build themselves.

blog-chetyre-funkczii-partnerskoj-dogovo.title: Why do partners need an agreement when they already have a charter?
blog-chetyre-funkczii-partnerskoj-dogovo.text: A partnership agreement does four jobs: declaring values, agreeing on scenarios, anchoring negotiations and enabling court enforcement. A charter and a shareholders' agreement cover only the fourth; the first three the partners can close only themselves.

scientia-4894.title: What work does a partners' agreement do besides court enforcement?
scientia-4894.text: Three others: declaring values, agreeing scenarios at the start and anchoring negotiations in disagreement; they work before any conflict and without the law. The state serves only the fourth function, court enforceability, and the article derives an order of work for co-owners.

li-7511363439181848576.title: What does a partnership document contain that a charter does not?
li-7511363439181848576.text: Two layers of three: relational (what is acceptable to the partners and what is not) and governance (who decides in disagreement, what happens on illness or exit). A lawyer drafts the legal layer but cannot write the first two for the partners: they hold agreements, not law.

blog-tri-sloya-partnerskogo-dokumenta-re.title: What are the three layers of a real partnership document?
blog-tri-sloya-partnerskogo-dokumenta-re.text: The relational layer records values and acceptable behaviour, the governance layer sets who decides and how, and the legal layer holds what a court will enforce. A standard charter has only the last one, so it is silent on contribution, disputes and a partner's illness.

li-7508514566788653056.title: How do agreement, document and contract differ?
li-7508514566788653056.text: An agreement is the consent people reach themselves, a document is its written record, and a contract is only the part you can take to court. The word "contract" sends partners to a lawyer before any agreement exists.

blog-dogovorennost-dokument-i-dogovor-tr.title: What three different things do partners call by the single word 'agreement'?
blog-dogovorennost-dokument-i-dogovor-tr.text: An understanding lives between people, a document records it, and a contract serves only court enforcement. Language glues the three into one word, so partners go looking for a contract where no understanding exists yet.

spilnota-5728.title: Why doesn't legal paperwork close the risk of conflict between partners?
spilnota-5728.text: Most of what partners must agree on is not a matter of law, so documents exist and conflicts remain. The abstract distinguishes three layers of agreement and marks where legal drafting ends; in Ukraine only 4.8% of problems respondents themselves saw as legal reach a court.

li-7505641269503676416.title: What is left of a partnership when there is a document but no agreement?
li-7505641269503676416.text: An empty form: a partnership agreement has three layers and four functions, and the law serves only court enforceability. Just 0.4% of civil cases in US federal courts reach trial, so "see you in court" is no plan but a long, costly end to the partnership.

blog-partnery-oformili-otnosheniya-poche.title: Why does making a partnership official not mean the partners have agreed?
blog-partnery-oformili-otnosheniya-poche.text: A charter and a shareholders' agreement describe how the company is structured, not how the partners will work together. Conflicts are triggered by a sense of unfairness rather than the numbers in a document, and most disputes never reach court.

zenodo-22748606.title: How much of a partnership agreement does the law actually serve?
zenodo-22748606.text: Only one of its four functions: judicial enforceability. The preprint separates agreement, document and contract, identifies three layers of a partnership agreement (relational, governance, legal) and shows why the word "contract" sends partners to a lawyer too early.
zenodo-22748606.o: Agreement Between Partners: Three Layers, Four Functions, and the Limit of Legal Formalization

li-7467102244379885568.title: What should five people who buy one Ferrari together agree on?
li-7467102244379885568.text: The author lists nine points: usage schedule and date clashes, servicing, costs, liability for damage, a reserve fund, a partner's exit, a right of first buyout, and death or incapacity. The exit scenario is the one most often forgotten, and conflicts start there.

li-7466405207325777920.title: Why is it so hard for partners to say what they actually want?
li-7466405207325777920.text: Few people can say exactly what they think, want, expect and refuse to accept, and in work with partners this is the hardest part. Until a thought is put into words, it cannot be discussed, agreed, disputed or written into an agreement.

li-7465350605159415808.title: How does LinkedIn judge an expert's professionalism?
li-7465350605159415808.text: A joke at the algorithm's expense: the network "knows best" what level the expert is at and who his ideal client is, suggesting a message to the boxer Usyk. A note on what automatic recommendations are worth.

li-7464565701614288897.title: When should partners review their agreements?
li-7464565701614288897.text: Regularly and before a crisis: once a partner unilaterally stops keeping them, the moment is lost. The author advises an annual check of roles, accumulated tension, financial arrangements and fairness of workload.

li-7463113890923593728.title: Why does AI make clients undervalue other people's work?
li-7463113890923593728.text: Without experience in the subject and with constant claims that AI does everything in two minutes, others' work seems worthless and redoing it seems free. The author's example: a client rejected a 16-page partnership proposal citing ChatGPT, and he ended the collaboration.

li-7462026751662264320.title: Will lawyers and the courts protect a partner?
li-7462026751662264320.text: Not reliably: in 2025 Ukrainian enforcement services collected 1.5 kopecks per hryvnia of debt, and only about 30% of claimants received real money. A strong partnership agreement exists to keep things out of court: conflict rules, mediation, a share-valuation formula.

li-7461334756929073152.title: What makes a person human: intelligence or the ability to break rules?
li-7461334756929073152.text: The author answers with irony: what makes behaviour human is breaking even signed rules for gain and convincing oneself that "I may this time". While AI just follows instructions, it is a tool.

tg-265.title: Which 20 questions should you ask a partner before you start?
tg-265.text: A list of 20 questions that show how a partner thinks, what they expect and want, and whether you match on values, goals and scale. For when the agreements at the start turned out shallow.

li-7454780901693026304.title: How does leadership in a partnership differ from leadership in business?
li-7454780901693026304.text: In business a leader manages a team; in a partnership, the partners' expectations. Such a leader keeps the dialogue going when others avoid sharp topics, takes responsibility for the relationship and builds a setting where co-owners can agree and renegotiate.

li-7453716252184936448.title: What is an idea worth and how should it count toward a partner's share?
li-7453716252184936448.text: An idea cannot be valued once and for all: its worth shifts with results, so a fixed price at the start is almost always wrong. Partners should agree on how an idea matures into a share, for instance through hypothesis-testing milestones.

tg-260.title: Where does a partner group's conflict come from: people or processes?
tg-260.text: In the processes: at a partnership session for a group of three it turned out the problem lay not between the partners but in business processes that systematically produced conflicts. The issue was resolved.

tg-259.title: What do entrepreneurs ask at a live meeting about partnership?
tg-259.text: About hard topics and real cases: at a meeting with entrepreneurs in Alicante the questions kept coming for three hours in the conference room and two more in a restaurant. The author calls live meetings the most energising format.

li-7451190897138036736.title: Why do only the already burned take a partnership agreement seriously?
li-7451190897138036736.text: A failed partnership makes people attentive to detail, future scenarios and the need to record agreements, while success relaxes them. The post cites that 25% of partnerships fall apart within three years, 30% by year five and 42% by year seven.

li-7448644935530139648.title: Where does a crisis in a partnership come from?
li-7448644935530139648.text: From the accumulated gap between "what we agreed" and "how things are": old roles, expectations and agreements run on inertia until the gap turns critical. Looking for a culprit is pointless: the rules went stale and no new ones were agreed.

li-7446089834881945600.title: How long does a partnership last without interest and respect for each other?
li-7446089834881945600.text: Not long: it quickly turns into an exchange of demands, and "he owes me" appears. In the author's view the question is not whether a partnership agreement is needed but whether it will be a living, dynamic structure or a paper that works only while things go well.

li-7443597164334768128.title: How does a professional show their level in a hard situation?
li-7443597164334768128.text: Pressure, uncertainty, conflict and the risk of loss push people to do something fast so it feels better. A professional is the one who stays clear-headed, holds the pause and thinks: the best decision is usually where there is more composure, not more action.

li-7442098229564985345.title: What helps a partnership get through turbulence?
li-7442098229564985345.text: Pre-agreed rules for unwelcome but foreseeable situations: who does what, how decisions are made, whether a reserve fund exists. When the answers are recorded, there is no need to negotiate from scratch; the partners simply follow the plan.

li-7441792849878073344.title: Who falls in love faster, and who falls harder: men or women?
li-7441792849878073344.text: A study in Springer Nature Biology finds that men realise they are in love about a month earlier, while women feel it more intensely, peaking at engagement and dropping sharply in the first two years of marriage. The author asks whether this carries over to business partnership.

li-7440662835661037568.title: Which crisis scenarios should a partnership agreement spell out in advance?
li-7440662835661037568.text: The agreement needs a separate chapter on crises: what happens to the share of a partner who stops delivering, how a partner who wants out leaves, who inherits the share in force majeure. Without answers fixed in advance, they get improvised under pressure and emotion.

li-7439267425537163264.title: Why are partners' starting expectations almost always too optimistic?
li-7439267425537163264.text: Even in SaaS only 3.3% of startups reach 1 million ARR within a year, 13.4% within three, 25.1% within five. One partner can wait 5-7 years without dividends, another expects payouts in 12-18 months, so goals and timing belong in the agreement, reviewed yearly.

li-7438494633426423808.title: What does a partner pay for entering a business on vague terms?
li-7438494633426423808.text: With freedom: by accepting unclear roles, undefined rules and a weak voice in decisions for the sake of money or a strong partner, he loses his say and his influence. It first looks like a compromise, then like dependence, and comfort bought with freedom rarely lasts.

li-7437031210461257728.title: Why does a partnership agreement need controlled pain?
li-7437031210461257728.text: Pain is a mechanism of accountability: with no chance of loss, promises come cheap and "we'll sort it out somehow" becomes a strategy. The agreement creates that pain through penalties, a share buyout, financial liability and a non-performance promissory note.

li-7436658452212391937.title: Why is a business built on one person no use to a partner or an investor?
li-7436658452212391937.text: Nearly all Michelin restaurants in Andalusia lose money: haute cuisine rests on the chef and has no scalable model. A business that depends on one partner's energy and contacts holds the investor hostage; a partner's value lies in building a system, not in overwork.

li-7434204725593690112.title: Where does the real value of a partnership session lie?
li-7434204725593690112.text: In the mental energy the agreements give back to the partners' business. While roles, money, power and rules remain unsettled, the brain keeps those questions running in the background, like peripheral vision in an optical illusion, and spends attention on them.

li-7433433091429384192.title: Why do partners ready to kill each other usually start as friends?
li-7433433091429384192.text: The author's client practice shows that almost every such case began with friendship and a belief that friends cannot have misunderstandings. The typical line: "Why do we need an agreement, we are reasonable people, we'll work it out."

li-7432811329884958720.title: Are partners born or made?
li-7432811329884958720.text: It seems being a partner is like being born a cat: you are born, and you are one. But a business partnership is a structure, logically and psychologically complex, with rules and methods of its own that have to be learned.

li-7432387983703453696.title: How can you test a professional in a field you know little about?
li-7432387983703453696.text: Ask 3-4 follow-up questions to every answer. A real professional relaxes, or says plainly that the thing you ask about does not exist; a pretender tenses up, fearing to be exposed.

li-7431669781130473472.title: Why does a business without an agreement end like a marriage without one?
li-7431669781130473472.text: There are 7 divorces per 10 marriages, in 80% of cases people cannot agree on their own, and fewer than 2% of couples sign a prenup. If love fails to settle it, money, power and ambition in business will not either; the author gives 5 reasons to sign at the start.

li-7428032757257306114.title: How is unpaid wages like being a co-owner with no access to the money?
li-7428032757257306114.text: At the start of 2026 Ukraine had 36,629 proceedings over unpaid wages, 6% more than a year earlier. A co-owner whose partners never agreed on payouts and dividends ends up in the same position: an owner on paper, without access to money in practice.

li-7426573116233023488.title: What does startup founders' giving up dating say about business partnerships?
li-7426573116233023488.text: If Silicon Valley founders optimise even romance for ROI, they are unlikely to treat shared money and responsibility differently. The author thinks the era of partnerships "between friends" is ending: what remains is a mature agreement with a contract, or chaos and conflict.

li-7423290392487313408.title: How close to reality is what partners do during conflicts?
li-7423290392487313408.text: A reader poll: the author says that what partners do during conflicts makes his blood run cold, and asks how close that impression is to reality.

li-7422968970770563072.title: Why did Napoleon leave business mail unopened for three weeks?
li-7422968970770563072.text: Over that time some matters resolved themselves, some lost relevance, some proved trivial. The author reads this as a lesson in managing attention: not everything that calls for a reaction now calls for a decision, and sometimes the best decision is to let time do its work.

li-7422608547793784832.title: What three parts does the author split a double-cross into?
li-7422608547793784832.text: Three stances: cross the other side first so they don't cross you; be the one crossed, suffer and seek satisfaction; or be the one who crosses and call the victims suckers. A note written in an ironic tone.

li-7421820678439534592.title: What does it mean when a partner is always too busy to discuss agreements?
li-7421820678439534592.text: In the author's view it is a sign you are not headed the same way: the partner has time for decisions and for spending money, but none for agreements. Agreements never revisited become convenient interpretations, and a partnership needs managing as a process of its own.

li-7421501310321188864.title: Why does working with people grow more valuable in the age of AI?
li-7421501310321188864.text: JPMorgan says critical thinking, emotional intelligence and the ability to hold a conversation become the key skills. In partnerships this held long before neural networks: an algorithm cannot see hidden motives, sense tension, or ask the awkward question in time.

li-7420054172638543873.title: What is the main result of working out partnership agreements?
li-7420054172638543873.text: Not the agreement itself but its second-order effects after signing: a predictable partner, less inner noise, faster decisions, operational trust, fewer conflicts. If partners find it easier to think and quicker to act after signing, the work was done right.

li-7419687574685786112.title: What is stronger than the market's invisible hand?
li-7419687574685786112.text: The visible hand of the regulator: the author, an economist by training, cites Trump's statement of 200% tariffs on French wine and champagne unless France joins the "Board of Peace". A single regulatory act overrides any self-regulation within a minute.

li-7419279629439451136.title: Why does the consultant first try to talk people out of partnership?
li-7419279629439451136.text: For the author partnership is a last resort, so he first checks whether a partnership session is needed at all and explains the difficulty, the work of managing the relationship and the risks. In about 20% of cases the partnership is not formed or ends after working with him.

li-7418913422186205185.title: How much have wage arrears in Ukraine grown since the full-scale war began?
li-7418913422186205185.text: By 20%: in October 2025 arrears reached 3.7 billion hryvnias, according to the State Statistics Service.

li-7418585872175898624.title: Why do clear agreements serve as rules of the game, not as a sign of distrust?
li-7418585872175898624.text: People respond to limits and opportunities: where something is allowed, someone will eventually use it. Asymmetries in influence, information and access to money, left unbalanced by agreements, end in grievances and conflict, while an agreement makes the relationship sturdier.

li-7417851762994221057.title: What does Ukrainians' record cash currency buying say about savings?
li-7417851762994221057.text: In 2025 Ukrainians bought almost 24 billion dollars in cash foreign currency, an all-time record; net purchases reached 6.83 billion. About 71% of operations are in dollars, 25% in euros, which the author reads as an effort to preserve what people have, not investment potential.

li-7417461601147985920.title: Who is to blame when a partner exploits your hardship to take the business?
li-7417461601147985920.text: The blame lies with the partner who exploited a dead end, but responsibility for leaving the relationship unformalised lies with you. Rules, authority, decision limits, control and an exit scenario should be fixed before starting, as in Jewish business culture.

li-7417180295403081728.title: How will people reach agreements if they cannot read and understand a page?
li-7417180295403081728.text: Teachers report that students cannot grasp a page of text, and reading as a habit has fallen 40% in ten years. The author asks how such people will read correspondence, rules and contracts: agreements grow more complex while the ability to record and keep them weakens.

li-7416744889301917696.title: How can partners catch tension in time?
li-7416744889301917696.text: The question is not whether there are problems (there always are) but how significant and sensitive they are for you: some argue and work on the next day, others store grievances for years. A regular check-up helps catch the moment before repair becomes too hard.

li-7416454302107574272.title: Does AI speed up experienced programmers?
li-7416454302107574272.text: No: in the study, experienced developers using a neural network worked 19% slower on average, although a quarter gain was expected. The prompt must be precise, the answer takes time, and the code has to be cleaned up before it can go into a real project.

li-7416381409516466176.title: How much did Ukraine earn from IT services exports in 11 months of 2025?
li-7416381409516466176.text: $5.97 billion, on average $543 million a month: up 2.4% year on year, yet 3% below 2021 and almost 10% below the 2022 record. IT makes up 42% of services exports and 12% of all exports, while total services exports fell 9%.

li-7416035520709091328.title: Where do adult decisions begin?
li-7416035520709091328.text: With an honest look at oneself. Complex theories, others' explanations and convenient excuses are accepted easily, but talk of one's own motives, fears and responsibility meets resistance, because the truth about oneself is almost always uncomfortable. It hurts, and it works.

li-7415678589020655616.title: What is compartmentalization and what does it cost a person?
li-7415678589020655616.text: Division into isolated compartments for functions, processes or information, found in biology, psychology and veterinary work. In the mind, it is keeping contradictory thoughts in separate boxes; the author argues comfortable living demands it, at some cost to human qualities.

li-7415294505433968640.title: Why do business partners still rely on chemistry and trust?
li-7415294505433968640.text: Among American Gen Z, 33% go on dates for a free meal and 38% would end a relationship over a partner's money problems. If even romance is counted in money and risk, the author asks, why do business partners count on "chemistry" instead of agreements?

li-7414553887283654656.title: Why is partnership data in Ukraine so hard to find?
li-7414553887283654656.text: A reader poll: the author collects first-hand data on business partnerships because almost no public statistics on co-owners exist in Ukraine.

li-7414207816640647168.title: Why is the partner who plays the hero a danger?
li-7414207816640647168.text: He works nights and plugs systemic gaps himself, then presents the lack of organisation as a unique contribution and demands a larger share. It ends in burnout, grievances and a fight for influence; the author advises writing each partner's involvement into the agreement.

li-7413844806126292993.title: In which cities of the world is the average salary highest?
li-7413844806126292993.text: In the list of average salaries in US dollars, Zurich (7788) and Geneva (7784) lead, followed by San Francisco (7092) and Chicago (5940); at the bottom are Warsaw (1609), Moscow (1499), Budapest (1442) and Athens (1417). The author asks where readers would move.

li-7411308210743160832.title: Who in Europe most often works 49 hours a week or more?
li-7411308210743160832.text: In the second quarter of 2025: Turkey 25.4%, Serbia 13.4%, Ukraine 11.6%, Poland 9.2%, Germany 4.4%. In a partnership, one partner's overwork without agreed hours and compensation quickly becomes a source of conflict and a claim to a larger share.

li-7410322595893596160.title: Which ranking did the author make it into at the end of 2025?
li-7410322595893596160.text: The author reports reaching the top 100 most effective Ukrainian-language authors, thanks the compiler of the ranking and says it is good to be among such company. A short personal note.

li-7410231252554915840.title: Where does big money come from, if not from everyone working harder?
li-7410231252554915840.text: Where people have agreed who takes the risk, who decides, who controls the capital and how the result is shared. Using Forbes data (Musk: +$333.2 billion in 2025), the author argues that AI platforms rest on tightly structured agreements.

li-7409132157622706176.title: What sets the ceiling of a partnership: the contract or the partners' skills?
li-7409132157622706176.text: The skills: a partnership cannot rise above the lowest level of partnership professionalism among its key partners. The four-level scale runs from intuitive to systemic; a signed agreement does not make a partnership systemic, it only amplifies what partners can already do.

li-7408770600313311232.title: How unevenly is wealth distributed in the world in 2025?
li-7408770600313311232.text: The top 10% of the population own 75% of personal wealth and receive 53% of income. The share of the richest 0.001% of adults rose from 3.8% in 1995 to 6.1% in 2025, and the top 1% captured 36.7% of the year's growth in global wealth.

li-7408070761325674496.title: How does one make sense of all this?
li-7408070761325674496.text: A caption to an image in the form of a single question: how to make sense of all this. The author gives no answer or explanation and leaves the question open to readers.

li-7407688012735807488.title: What do you really choose when you choose a partner?
li-7407688012735807488.text: Someone who will influence the money, the power and decisions, the speed of the business and you yourself. The key question is not whether he is great but whether you are ready to share influence and whether rules limit it: without agreements, one partner always grows stronger.

li-7407332337455095809.title: Why can a simple wording reveal the depth of a problem?
li-7407332337455095809.text: Sometimes a simple wording lights up the full depth of a problem, but reaching such simplicity takes a long road. A short comment by the author on someone else's thought.

li-7406951341778161664.title: Why is it so hard to find statistics on partnerships?
li-7406951341778161664.text: A reader poll: the author notes that finding statistics on partnerships is harder than the proverbial search for an unknown place, and tries to tackle the problem by putting a question to his audience.

li-7406594038713430016.title: Why have a future partner profiled before the deal?
li-7406594038713430016.text: A partnership collapses not because someone cheated someone but because nobody worked out who was sitting across the table. A profiler shows behaviour under pressure and over money; a partnership session then fixes obligations, shares and rules before signing.

li-7406227203559985152.title: Why did a Spanish court uphold a dismissal for arriving half an hour early?
li-7406227203559985152.text: A court in Alicante treated as serious misconduct the fact that a 22-year-old logistics employee came in half an hour early: undermining discipline, disrupting teamwork, risking conflict. The author recalls partners who are "always and everywhere", but calls that another story.

li-7405524244685815808.title: Are social networks and algorithms to blame for the demand for fast and short?
li-7405524244685815808.text: No, the author argues: content without depth or context is the consumer's choice, as clients want everything yesterday and for next to nothing. He distrusts anyone promising a quick fix for complex problems and calls that kind of thinking childish magical thinking.

li-7404081240879898624.title: When does a mistake become a problem for a partnership?
li-7404081240879898624.text: When it is hidden, denied or shifted onto others; a mistake that is openly discussed and fixed becomes an asset and experience. For a partnership the key question is not how to avoid errors but whether partners are ready to correct quickly, agree and renegotiate.

li-7402256782011695105.title: What will the first official lobbyists change in Ukraine?
li-7402256782011695105.text: The NACP transparency register now lists 108 lobbyists; the first test is the January 2026 reports, which will show whether this is a tool of transparent influence or a screen for old schemes. For a partnership organiser, a lobbyist is a carrier of social capital.

li-7401914940409753600.title: Is there any partnership data in Ukraine?
li-7401914940409753600.text: A reader poll: according to the author, nobody collects statistics on partnerships worldwide, and certainly not in Ukraine, and he tries to solve the problem by starting with a question to his audience.

li-7401167242069016578.title: Who studied more before founding a unicorn: men or women?
li-7401167242069016578.text: Women. A Stanford analysis of 3,131 unicorn founders (199 of them women) found MBA or PhD as the highest degree in 45% of women and 39% of men, with bachelor's levels almost equal.

li-7399716017033187328.title: Why agree on an exit from the business before it even starts?
li-7399716017033187328.text: Just as an investor works out the exit before entering a project, partners need a separation scenario in advance, or the exit becomes a war. The partnership agreement should fix how shares are valued, buyout terms, scenario options and timelines.

li-7399399388684558337.title: Why is there almost no statistics on partnerships?
li-7399399388684558337.text: A reader poll: the author argues that partnership statistics are missing because nobody collects them, least of all in Ukraine, and tries to fill the gap with data of his own.

li-7398629119841832960.title: Which year in the past 20 produced the most of today's active unicorns?
li-7398629119841832960.text: 2015: it accounts for 10% of the 1,691 US-founded unicorns in a Stanford GSB analysis. The 2022-2024 cohorts give only 1% each, since reaching unicorn status historically takes about 7 years.

li-7396453996615421952.title: Why do business partners need a "prenup"?
li-7396453996615421952.text: Partners need an agreement on how they part ways, discussed at the start while the relationship is warm rather than when someone is already slamming the door. It is not distrust but a way to keep respect when the business has to be divided.

li-7396087871071395840.title: Is the era of easy entry into venture capital over?
li-7396087871071395840.text: A study by Strebulaev and Jackson of 10,316 junior VC professionals in the US (2000-2025) shows the inflow of newcomers rising to a 2022 peak, then falling to 509 by 2025, half that level. Capital is costlier and funds more cautious.

li-7395393421038911489.title: Why shouldn't you put inspiration off until later?
li-7395393421038911489.text: Inspiration has an expiry date: it does not return in the same form, and an unused idea will either die or be built by someone else. Even a small step helps: write it down, draw it, play it.

li-7394740471643697153.title: Do public declarations match practice, in the case of Kiyosaki?
li-7394740471643697153.text: Kiyosaki taught saving and investing, yet admitted to $1.2 billion of debt to banks and says it is now the banks' problem. The author passes no moral verdict but notes that there are flawed and effective methods, and public declarations versus actual behaviour.

li-7394277958233915392.title: Which five illusions destroy partnerships?
li-7394277958233915392.text: Partners believe the partnership is solid until the first cracks appear, while problems ripen under verbal trust and outdated agreements. A partnership is not a contract signed once but a living organism that needs reviews, transparency, hard talks and renegotiation.

li-7392828929247637504.title: Is every conflict with a partner worth the nerves?
li-7392828929247637504.text: No: not every conflict is worth the nervous energy, not every partner is ready to agree, not every situation deserves another chance. Sometimes peace means leaving a game where your balance is constantly tested.

li-7392463526667296770.title: Does the author have a business and partnership experience of his own?
li-7392463526667296770.text: Yes: 15 years of partnership experience and, since 2020, a wholesale trade in fresh fruit and vegetables. The business is operational and depends on the partner who is its CEO; the author regularly goes out to the fields to keep tasting it.

li-7392101314282831873.title: What does the Beckham documentary reveal about him as a businessman?
li-7392101314282831873.text: Football never gripped the author; people do: motives, thinking patterns, ways of reaching goals. Four episodes on David Beckham showed him to be a strong businessman too, and his main commercial project gets a separate breakdown.

li-7391530372188172288.title: How did the author find working with the audience at an event?
li-7391530372188172288.text: A thank-you to the event organisers: the author calls working with the audience a pure pleasure.

li-7391373416773308416.title: Which 10 facts about business partnerships does the author see in his work?
li-7391373416773308416.text: A set of ten facts about business partnerships that the author regularly observes in his own practice.

li-7391100005329215489.title: Does the theme of partnership resonate with successful professionals?
li-7391100005329215489.text: The author is glad to see that the subject he devotes himself to resonates with people who have succeeded in their own professional fields.

li-7391012179082227712.title: What do you do when a partner suddenly asks for a bigger share?
li-7391012179082227712.text: The problem is neither the shares nor the partner but the lack of an agreement and a worked-out scenario: a change of shares is a "known unknown". An annual preventive partnership session reconciles contributions and expectations, so the request is no surprise.

li-7389563830894342144.title: What does evil in a partnership look like?
li-7389563830894342144.text: Rarely as loud conflicts or theft, more as a slow, barely visible corrosion of trust: petty manipulation, excuses, pressure just to win. One day the person beside you is no partner but someone systematically harming the business, the relationship and you.

li-7389195984808882176.title: What three kinds of capital do partners bring to a shared business?
li-7389195984808882176.text: Economic, human and social: money and assets, knowledge and experience, reputation and connections. The author gives each a key question, and a tilt toward one kind leads to control and fear, stagnation or chaos.

li-7388833298250162176.title: How can partners settle disputes without going to court?
li-7388833298250162176.text: Step by step: regular meetings outside operations, a formal notice of the dispute, a meeting of partners without lawyers, a neutral arbiter, and only then mediation, arbitration or court. The author calls court a defeat: costly and years long.

li-7388471345325441024.title: What does it cost to build a unicorn, and what has partnership to do with it?
li-7388471345325441024.text: For a valuation above $1 billion a company raises $340 million on average (median $250 million). But investors also examine how the partnership is built: roles, decision mechanisms, agreements for disagreements. This is trust capital.

li-7387744792782311425.title: Why does expecting a perfect partner lead to neurosis?
li-7387744792782311425.text: Idealisation first inspires, then paralyses: it brings disappointment in whatever misses the picture, or endless effort to bend the world to your standards. A partner's strength is working with imperfection and agreeing despite flaws.

li-7387007577689227264.title: Is giving the CEO a share of the business a fitting reward?
li-7387007577689227264.text: Handing over a share is not a thank-you but the end point of a path on which trust was built. Trust is an economic category: it is either earned or not. The author met this at two partner meetings where owners wanted to "reward" the CEO.

li-7386642520425959425.title: Who systematically collects data on partnerships?
li-7386642520425959425.text: A reader poll: by the author's account, nobody but him systematically collects such data, and this latest question is part of that collection.

li-7386278013547671553.title: What is partners' biggest mistake when they part ways?
li-7386278013547671553.text: Not agreeing in advance on the value of the business and the shares. Partners sometimes spell out how to separate but not for how much, and it is the valuation that breaks the deal, drags out months of stress and then court.

li-7386004243201015809.title: Who might you find behind the wheel of a taxi in Spain?
li-7386004243201015809.text: A light note from a trip: the taxi driver in Spain turned out to be a Spaniard, and the author says he dreams of meeting the driver's parents.

li-7385927874832138241.title: What is partnership, put without the big words?
li-7385927874832138241.text: Partnership is when "what suits me" gives way to "what is better for us". Agreements are not only about roles, money and shares but about taming ambition, fear and the urge to grab more; opportunism is natural, and negotiating teaches partners to act together.

li-7384460634890874880.title: Does a written exit mechanism help founders keep control of the company?
li-7384460634890874880.text: Yes: in Carta's 2024 report, 72% of founders with a written exit mechanism kept control of the company after a split, against only 38% of those without one. The question is not trust in the partner but readiness for any scenario.

li-7384181826313064448.title: What happens to a business when a founder leaves with nothing agreed?
li-7384181826313064448.text: According to Carta, in 68% of companies with no exit mechanisms, one founder leaving leads to a management crisis or a complete freeze. An exit plan is needed not in case of betrayal but in case of life.

li-7383753139709018112.title: Why are most co-owner conflicts not about money?
li-7383753139709018112.text: They are about expectations: per Carta, over 80% of founders launch without a formal agreement. Who decides, who has the last word on a sale, when dividends are paid: without written rules, emotions settle all of it.

li-7383392014093926400.title: How often does the founding team change in the first five years?
li-7383392014093926400.text: Per Carta, 53% of companies with several founders change their co-founder lineup within the first five years. Partnerships break up over differences in pace and goals and plain fatigue, so mature founders plan for parting as well as growth.

li-7382699263555973120.title: What is an honest agreement worth in a world that prizes image?
li-7382699263555973120.text: In a world where public image outranks reputation and promises outweigh deeds, an honest signed agreement becomes a luxury. Only mature partners can afford it.

li-7382325985448325120.title: How does a partner know they are valued?
li-7382325985448325120.text: By four signs, not by kind words: agreements are kept, time and contribution are respected, results are recorded and acknowledged, and respect holds under tension. A partner who feels superfluous will sooner or later leave.

li-7381956477982273536.title: Why do partner meetings decay into gatherings about nothing?
li-7381956477982273536.text: Partners meet tired at day's end, each busy with their own work, conclude "we're fine", then pause for months. Meetings exist for relationships, synchronisation and refining the rules; problem cases, scenarios, contributions and agreements cannot be settled on the run.

li-7381215587466743808.title: What keeps a partnership going once the emotions fade?
li-7381215587466743808.text: Only agreements do. Emotions drive the start but blind partners to the need for rules, and a year or two later yesterday's believers talk through lawyers. The cure is agreements fixed in advance: roles, decisions, what happens on exit, how profit and loss are shared.

li-7380853200112918528.title: How often do Ukrainians found billion-dollar companies?
li-7380853200112918528.text: Ukraine ranks 10th in the world by number of unicorn founders (12) and 6th per capita, at 0.32 per million people. The data come from Ilya Strebulaev's Stanford research; the author asks how to turn individual strength into a systemic advantage for the country.

li-7380142983050002432.title: Should a business partner be replaced every 8 years?
li-7380142983050002432.text: The author applies the rule "a maximum of 8 years in power", built on the idea that even the best eventually become dictators, to a business partner, a wife and friends. If the rule is universal it always works; if not, the "expiry date" of leaders is in doubt.

li-7379764372996259840.title: May the partner who runs finances pay dividends to himself first?
li-7379764372996259840.text: In the author's view, no: control of the money is a test of trust. Payouts go either to everyone at once by share, or first to those without access to the accounts. In a client case, years of this practice ended in a serious conflict.

li-7379403347948281856.title: What protects a business better from a departing partner?
li-7379403347948281856.text: A ban on poaching clients and staff (no-poach, no-solicit) protects in practice and is almost always enforceable, while a full non-compete is often too harsh and barely works in some places. With no agreement, a partner's exit from an IT firm cost it 60% of revenue in a year.

li-7379032320781152256.title: Who collects statistics on partnership?
li-7379032320781152256.text: A reader poll: the author says no statistics on partnership exist and that he alone collects them systematically, so he puts a question to the audience to gather his own data.

tg-141.title: What is happening to the restaurant business?
tg-141.text: A one-line remark by the author, phrased as a question, about how the restaurant business is faring; the post gives no answer or explanation.

li-7378679035377315840.title: How do you assess your social capital for a partnership?
li-7378679035377315840.text: Social capital is a contribution on a par with money and skills: reputation, contacts and audience, ability to create opportunities. Five steps: list key contacts, recall whom you introduced, where your reputation got you invited, who asked your advice, what you can add today.

tg-139.title: Is partnership a rocket or a minefield?
tg-139.text: A podcast episode on what partners usually leave unsaid: why the agreement comes before big plans, how to discuss exit while all is well, what to do when contributions are unequal but shares equal, how to keep trust when one partner has a baby and another a new investor.

li-7378043277402353664.title: What root problems arise when a partner group is formed?
li-7378043277402353664.text: The author shares a light but substantive dialogue on the root problems of forming a partner group. His comment: be realistic, agree boldly, and be ready to renegotiate in the future.

li-7377228388652027904.title: Why do most partnerships fall apart?
li-7377228388652027904.text: Because nobody manages them: agreeing at the start is not management. Agreements must be revisited: review the economics and roles, track partnership metrics, run plan-versus-actual and scenario planning, and keep tools for resolving conflicts.

li-7376864675340107776.title: Why does consensus get in the way of partners' decisions?
li-7376864675340107776.text: Consensus blurs decisions, slows them, dilutes accountability, kills strong ideas and creates false agreement. Following Alastair Rampell's "Conviction beats consensus", the author advises agreeing who leads in which area and who decides when views differ.

li-7376495714702483456.title: Does any statistics on partnership exist?
li-7376495714702483456.text: A reader poll: the author claims no statistics on partnership exist and nobody but him collects them systematically, and asks the audience a question to obtain data of his own.

li-7376142761214885888.title: When is it right to deliberately turn down a client who haggles?
li-7376142761214885888.text: When the client demands the same work faster: haggling builds inflated expectations, and agreeing to a shorter term can cost more than the fee, in reputation and negative feedback. The author recalls the saying that nine women cannot bear a child in a month.

li-7374693674531713025.title: How does the founders' agreement affect a startup's valuation?
li-7374693674531713025.text: Investors dislike surprises, and these usually come from co-founders: without clear agreements the risk of conflict and of a sudden departure grows. A signed partnership agreement shows an investor rules of the game, predictability and maturity.

li-7373966519824904192.title: Why is the author collecting his own statistics on partnerships?
li-7373966519824904192.text: A reader poll: no statistics on business partnership exist, so the author gathers data on the Ukrainian segment himself, one short question at a time.

li-7373605278178705408.title: What can a partner do after leaving a business with no exit agreement?
li-7373605278178705408.text: A departed co-owner can leave payables, keep receivables, start a rival firm, take clients, team and IP. The answer: agree in advance on a one-year ban on competing and poaching, share valuation, escrow rules and a buyout term.

li-7373241991268024320.title: How can Ukrainian startups get enough funding to reach unicorn scale?
li-7373241991268024320.text: Crunchbase data show a typical startup raises about $340M before a $1B valuation, while Ukrainian rounds in 2025 stay at pre-seed and seed. It takes new funds, large cheques and long work, including on relations between founders.

li-7371794695716413442.title: Why doesn't profit save a partnership that is not managed?
li-7371794695716413442.text: Open conflict is preceded by a string of omissions: no regular syncs, no review of contributions and expectations, no interaction rules, no transparent reporting, no meetings about the partnership itself. Managing the relationship is a separate process worth investing in.

li-7371422291022413824.title: What does the author want to learn from readers about partnerships?
li-7371422291022413824.text: Another poll in a series: there is no data on partnerships, so the author keeps collecting it in the Ukrainian business segment and puts a new question to readers.

li-7371066106914103297.title: When is a proposed partnership worth walking away from?
li-7371066106914103297.text: When shares are set with no calculation rule, an investor making the full financial contribution gets the same as the producer, and experts lose control of their IP with no way to revisit terms. That is what one draft agreement on an info product looked like.

li-7370703102850719744.title: Could digital dopamine kill the need for business partnership as well?
li-7370703102850719744.text: An Institute for Family Studies report: weekly sexual activity among US adults fell from 55% in 1990 to 37% in 2024. Partnership, like intimacy, rests on regular time and attention; the author leaves the question open to readers.

li-7369619009803010048.title: What place did theatre have in the author's life?
li-7369619009803010048.text: Theatre was an outlet: first as a spectator, then as a performer. The author recalls his two years at the Black Square theatre studio with warmth.

li-7369258478638473216.title: Why do a partner's other skills turn harmful without basic decency?
li-7369258478638473216.text: If partners have not learned agreement, honesty and mutual responsibility, every other skill works against them: finance without honesty becomes manipulation, sales without accountability erodes trust, legal knowledge without ethics sets traps in contracts.

li-7368893036904349696.title: Is there any statistics on business partnerships in Ukraine?
li-7368893036904349696.text: No, and that is why the author keeps collecting data himself. This is one more reader poll in the Ukrainian business audience.

li-7368533975268503555.title: Can you trust a partner who dodges clear answers at the start?
li-7368533975268503555.text: No. In a project partnership example, an agency wanted a 5,000 euro prepayment plus 30% of the grant, gave no answer to clear questions and left the talks. The clients saved months and at least 5,000 euros.

li-7368166344657235971.title: Can partners from generations X, Y and Z work well together?
li-7368166344657235971.text: Only if agreements stop being verbal promises. The Understanding America Study shows neuroticism rising and conscientiousness and sociability falling among young Americans, while partnership needs obligations, planning and the ability to admit mistakes.

li-7367082095631835136.title: Does talent guarantee success in a partnership?
li-7367082095631835136.text: No: talent shows how fast one learns, while success depends on the number of attempts times the odds of each. Without focus, readiness to experiment and the will to act, even a talented partner remains only potential.

li-7366356308846899200.title: Why collect data on partnerships in Ukraine single-handedly?
li-7366356308846899200.text: No statistics on partnership exist, and the author decided to change something in this field on his own. The reader poll continues his data-gathering series.

li-7365995617644343298.title: What risks does a "sleeping" partner face, and how can they be reduced?
li-7365995617644343298.text: Five risks: theft or corruption, unapproved disposal of assets, hidden costs, "creative" reporting, and lost control of key contracts and clients. The remedy is revisiting the agreement and a regular audit by an auditor the sleeping partner chooses.

li-7364921844191113218.title: Is a partner a resource or a party to a system of agreements?
li-7364921844191113218.text: For pragmatic traders a partner is a resource, and a project's profit is inversely proportional to the partner's experience. For mature entrepreneurs, partnership is a system of agreements, a balance of contributions and mutual responsibility.

li-7364545997747769344.title: Which three principles keep a partnership intact even in a crisis?
li-7364545997747769344.text: Agree in advance to renegotiate; openly acknowledge roles and contributions out loud; own your subjectivity, speaking directly and for yourself even in conflict. The principles come from the author's practice since his first partnership agreement in 2016.

li-7363819588989468673.title: What is known about partnerships in Ukrainian business?
li-7363819588989468673.text: Almost nothing: there is no partnership statistics, so the author keeps gathering data through polls of readers in the Ukrainian segment.

li-7363459480295981056.title: Why must partners renegotiate their agreements regularly?
li-7363459480295981056.text: Business, market and partners' goals change, and freezing terms instead of adapting breeds resentment or silence. Revisiting is maturity, not betrayal: set a review date, make open and reasoned proposals, and be ready to admit mistakes and changed context.

li-7363094672820391937.title: How can a partner be held accountable for broken promises?
li-7363094672820391937.text: The author advises non-performance promissory notes: partners issue each other notes for an agreed sum, payable on set triggers such as vanishing for a month, missing a KPI or not reporting for a quarter. It is financial accountability, like alimony in a family.

li-7361649103702765568.title: Why is a populist among partners dangerous?
li-7361649103702765568.text: Partners answer jointly: one makes the promise, everyone cleans up. In the case discussed it ended in a quarrel, lost counterparties and a halted business. Agree on who may promise what, to whom and when, and write failure scenarios down in advance.

li-7361283217271812096.title: When are partners' actions in a business empty?
li-7361283217271812096.text: When they do not fit the situation: a three-year strategy with no agreement on contributions, brainstorms amid passive aggression, shared management imitated while one person decides. A partnership session for full synchronisation tests them against reality.

li-7360921771904004096.title: Can AI replace shared thinking between partners?
li-7360921771904004096.text: No: AI can analyse and suggest options, but it will not take a risk with a partner, accept responsibility or stand by them in a hard moment. At a partnership session, one of three co-founders stopped consulting the others, having thought it all through with ChatGPT.

tg-118.title: Why do venture funds look for partners with an MBA less and less?
tg-118.text: In 2000 every second senior investment partner in venture capital held an MBA; in 2025 only 36 % do. Funds now look for technology knowledge, founder experience and industry depth: what matters is the value a partner can bring, not where they studied.

li-7360559069956403200.title: What matters more in a partner: an MBA or experience?
li-7360559069956403200.text: Experience. In 2000 every second senior investment partner in venture capital held an MBA; in 2025 only 36% do. The key question is not where a partner studied but what value they can bring today and tomorrow.

li-7356205671849037825.title: How do you explain what you do so that people remember it?
li-7356205671849037825.text: Instead of "I work with business partnerships" the author says: I help co-owners reach agreement before the big problems start. He then names the steps: interviews, a partnership session, roles and decision rules, a partnership agreement.

li-7355851613384675331.title: Why doesn't trust between partners replace structure?
li-7355851613384675331.text: Without structure, trust turns into chaos: one partner decides for the other or nothing gets decided, and responsibility hangs somewhere in a chat. The author starts every case by asking who is in charge, then checks who answers for what and who has the final say.

li-7355488919217463296.title: At what age and with what experience do people enter venture capital?
li-7355488919217463296.text: A Stanford GSB study finds that 42 % of US venture investors entered the field at 20–29, 38 % at 30–39 and 7 % after 50; the median age is 31. For most it is not a first job: 7 % had built their own companies and 11 % had worked at startups.

li-7354407067127791617.title: What is stability built on if income and a business can vanish?
li-7354407067127791617.text: On the ability to create value: how you think, how you decide and whether anyone will pay for it. Partners choose each other for the capacity to create shared value, and if such a partner remains, a business can be rebuilt from a blank page.

li-7353311739297382400.title: When did you last meet your partner to work on the partnership itself?
li-7353311739297382400.text: Advisorpedia experts say that without regular meetings strategy and communication begin to erode. An annual partnership session fixes areas of responsibility, compensation for contributions and roles for the year; 5–6 hours a year guard against conflict and burnout.

li-7352949432964866048.title: Why does demographic decline make partnership a way for business to survive?
li-7352949432964866048.text: In the first half of 2025 Ukraine recorded 86,795 births and 249,002 deaths; the population shrinks by about 300,000 a year. With fewer workers and entrepreneurs, and scale impossible alone, partnership becomes a way to survive and grow.

li-7351498404834738177.title: Why can a partner's age be an advantage rather than a drawback?
li-7351498404834738177.text: Mature partners are less likely to break down, fight less for being right and more for results, and know the context and what definitely not to do. Someone over 40 who has been through several cycles brings composure and depth, not only speed, within limits, the author adds.

li-7351129646760898560.title: Why do agreements free people rather than restrict them?
li-7351129646760898560.text: When everything is spoken through and written down, nobody has to recall earlier decisions, keep it all in their head or debate whether to speak up. Each person knows their responsibility, the norm and the red line: the more clarity, the less drama.

li-7350775510928367616.title: How do you split shares when "equal for everyone" does not work?
li-7350775510928367616.text: Partners rate how much human, social and economic capital each contributes, the ratings are averaged and applied to a third of the circle. In the example, ratings of 100 % and 90 % give the partner 95 % of economic capital, which is a 31.35 % share.

li-7350412120682827776.title: Why should partners avoid taking a dispute to court?
li-7350412120682827776.text: A judge is no entrepreneur or partner and carries no commercial risk, so will not grasp the situation from inside. The author offers an agreement with no blank spots, plus a contrast: a judge's average pension is about UAH 107,000, an average Ukrainian's UAH 5,800.

li-7349368747356217344.title: Why do startups fail over agreements rather than over the idea?
li-7349368747356217344.text: In the author's view the main cause of startup collapse is neither the idea nor the market but the agreements between partners. The foundation is roles, shares, areas of responsibility, the right to exit and likely future scenarios.

li-7348965461474078720.title: Which three entrepreneurial styles does a strong partnership need?
li-7348965461474078720.text: Gallup's Builder Profile 10 names three styles, Activation, Relational and Strategic; an ideal partnership needs all of them. Two strategists never reach execution, two activators give motion without system, and relational types alone give agreements but nothing built.

li-7348656544957227010.title: How do power and fairness combine in a strong partnership?
li-7348656544957227010.text: Power without fairness becomes dictatorship; fairness without power is a toothless dream. One partner takes the lead, the others know the rules and are honest: a strong partnership rests on balanced power and agreed fairness, not equality in everything.

li-7348237232341671936.title: When is it better not to form a partnership at all?
li-7348237232341671936.text: When a partner is treated as a function rather than an equal. In the case described, a well-known blogger wants only a producer's expertise while she wants a business of her own, so there is no psychological contract. The advice: hire and pay, but do not call it partnership.

li-7347874655472357376.title: How should a business in Ukraine be built given demographic change?
li-7347874655472357376.text: The author cites figures: Ukraine lost 40 % of its working-age population between 2021 and 2023, 74 % of employers feel a labour shortage, and by 2035 81 % of the population will be over 45. He asks readers how they plan to build a business under these conditions.

li-7346484013408104448.title: Why can't a partnership rest on plans and spreadsheets alone?
li-7346484013408104448.text: Without inspiration even simple things stall: with trust, common ground and drive partners withstand any chaos, while without energy an ordinary meeting ends in hurt feelings. That inner fire has to be maintained and invested in.

li-7346064757851848704.title: How do you win over the other side in a negotiation?
li-7346064757851848704.text: Four moves: back your words with facts and stories without embellishing, listen actively and do not interrupt, show respect like an advocate rather than a prosecutor, and see the other side's gain without losing your own. Keep the substance, not the form.

li-7345761158928261120.title: What makes a stronger brand: being public or staying private?
li-7345761158928261120.text: The author looks at the company that organised Jeff Bezos's wedding: its site has no social media or work examples, only talk of confidentiality. He asks which brand is stronger, public or private, and invites colleagues to judge its GTM, brand strategy and design.

li-7345701075313684480.title: Why is an honest assessment of yourself so hard to get and to hear?
li-7345701075313684480.text: James O'Toole holds that the more power a partner has, the less they listen; subordinates hold back, and family and friends see one side. Partners watch you at work and want you effective, so their feedback at a partnership session is especially valuable.

li-7345337670530650116.title: What do a godfather and a business partner have in common?
li-7345337670530650116.text: Trust is never "a little" or "in words": it is handing over what is dearest without guarantees. A partner takes on a "child", the shared business, and it holds not on contracts alone but on whether he stays when it gets hard and speaks honestly when something goes wrong.

li-7343889478861606913.title: How do you keep a partnership together when partners see things differently?
li-7343889478861606913.text: Start not by proving you are right but by describing what you feel, and treat your own position as a hypothesis to be tested. When partners try to prove a point the ego wins and the business often loses; strong partners tell emotion from decision.

li-7343525043659857923.title: Is it wise to look for a partner with a spotless record?
li-7343525043659857923.text: "He never had a single conflict" often only means the person never held a decisive role: never signed, never risked, never answered for anything. The author advises looking not for the spotless but for those who went through hardship and drew conclusions.

li-7343164308035358720.title: How did four partnerships lead the author to partnership agreements?
